newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen leader wants talks with Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Chechen leader wants talks with Yeltsin.

text.p: The leader of Russia's breakaway region of Chechnya, Aslan Maskhadov, said on Thursday he was ready to meet President Boris Yeltsin to discuss relations between Moscow and Grozny, Interfax news agency said.
Interfax quoted Maskhadov as saying that he wanted to discuss with Yeltsin a full-scale political pact which would grant the separatist region wider formal powers.
Maskhadov's remarks came a day after Yeltsin clearly indicated he was not going to discuss any deal which would give Chechnya any other status than that of a part of the vast Russian federation.
Yeltsin, who is vacationing on the River Volga, said on Wednesday he was willing to meet Maskhadov.

He said it was good time to strike a power-sharing deal with Chechnya similar to those the Kremlin has with other Russian regions, but ruled out signing any document which might be interpreted as recognition of Chechnya's independence.
"My plan is that we should prepare a power-sharing agreement. That's what we need at this stage," he said. "But if we talk about a full-scale document we are not ready for it."
Chechen deputy premier Movladi Udugov said on Wednesday that Grozny for its part would not accept any deal which could be interpreted as acknowledgement of the region remaining part of Russia.
Maskhadov also said negotiations at lower levels between Chechen and Russian ministries had failed to produce implementation of earlier agreements between Russia and Chechnya.
Tension between Moscow and Grozny grew earlier this week when the Chechen authorities accused Russia of reneging on a promise to fund reconstruction in the war-devastated region.
Maskhadov told his ministers on Tuesday to halt all discussions with Moscow other than top-level talks until a comprehensive document on reconstruction was worked out.
Chechen leaders, who signed a peace deal with Moscow last August after ousting Russian troops from Grozny, insist that their predominantly Moslem region in the Caucasus is independent from Russia.
Under the deal, the question of formal sovereignty was set aside until 2001. As a part of the peace deal, the Kremlin pledged to plough in funds to rebuild Chechnya's economy and infrastructure.
